species.name: Asian small-clawed otter
species.habitat: Mangroves, freshwater wetlands, streams and muddy banks
species.rarity: Rare in Singapore and much less often seen than the smooth-coated otter
species.sourceName: Animal Diversity Web · University of Michigan
species.summary: The world's smallest otter species, with dexterous front paws used to feel for small prey. It must not be confused with Singapore's larger, more familiar smooth-coated otter.
species.identification: A small dark-brown otter with a pale throat, short claws that do not extend beyond the fingertips and partly webbed paws. Size alone is not enough for a confident identification.
species.diet: Crabs, molluscs and other aquatic invertebrates, along with frogs and small fish.
species.activity: Can forage by day or night depending on disturbance, prey and local conditions.
species.behaviour: Social and vocal, often foraging with sensitive paws in mud and shallow water. Family groups use dens and scent-marked areas.
species.reproduction: A pair may raise a small litter with help from older group members. General species biology does not identify a Singapore den or breeding date.
species.singapore: NParks lists the native Asian small-clawed otter as Critically Endangered. Any suspected record should be documented from a distance and checked by specialists.
species.ecologicalRole: A predator of crabs, molluscs and other small wetland animals, linking shallow water and bank habitats.
species.pressures: Wetland loss, water pollution, road traffic, disturbance and illegal wildlife trade affect small-clawed otters across their range.
species.watch: Keep a wide distance, dogs leashed and the route to water clear. Never feed otters or share the location of a den.
species.fact: Its sensitive, partly webbed paws help it feel for prey in mud and shallow water.

species.name: Cave nectar bat
species.habitat: Caves, forest edges, orchards, gardens and flowering trees
species.rarity: Uncommon and mainly detected at night or at roosts
species.sourceName: Animal Diversity Web · University of Michigan
species.summary: A long-snouted fruit bat specialised for feeding at flowers. By carrying pollen between plants, it provides an important nocturnal pollination service.
species.identification: A medium-sized brown fruit bat with a long narrow muzzle, large eyes and a short tail. Its tongue and muzzle suit feeding from deep flowers.
species.diet: Nectar and pollen, with soft fruit also eaten.
species.activity: Nocturnal; leaves the day roost after dusk to visit flowering plants.
species.behaviour: Roosts communally in caves or cave-like shelter and can travel several kilometres while feeding. It does not use laryngeal echolocation like many insect-eating bats.
species.reproduction: Females normally bear a single young and nurse it. Regional reproductive timing must not be treated as a fixed Singapore calendar.
species.singapore: NParks lists the cave nectar bat as native and Vulnerable. Feeding records around flowering trees do not identify or disclose a sensitive roost.
species.ecologicalRole: A night-time pollinator of forest and cultivated plants, moving pollen between widely separated flowers.
species.pressures: Disturbance or loss of communal roosts, removal of flowering trees and persecution can harm colonies and their pollination role.
species.watch: Never enter or light a bat roost. Watch feeding bats from a distance, keep cats indoors at night and do not handle a grounded bat.
species.fact: Pollen carried on its fur helps fertilise flowers visited after dark.

species.name: Common treeshrew
species.habitat: Forest, secondary woodland, plantations and wooded parks
species.rarity: Locally present in suitable woodland but easily overlooked
species.sourceName: Animal Diversity Web · University of Michigan
species.summary: A quick, squirrel-like mammal of the forest floor and low branches. It is neither a true shrew nor a squirrel, despite the familiar comparisons.
species.identification: A pointed snout, large eyes, rounded ears and a long bushy tail. A pale shoulder stripe helps distinguish it from similarly sized squirrels.
species.diet: Insects and other small animals, together with fruit and other plant food.
species.activity: Diurnal, with much foraging carried out on the ground and low vegetation.
species.behaviour: Moves rapidly along logs, leaf litter and branches. Individuals use scent marking and defended home areas.
species.reproduction: The species has small litters in a nest. Mothers use an unusual brief nursing pattern between visits; this is general biology, not a Singapore breeding calendar.
species.singapore: NParks lists the common treeshrew as native and Least Concern nationally. It depends on vegetated habitat even when a record comes from near a park edge.
species.ecologicalRole: An omnivore that eats small invertebrates and fruit, linking several parts of the forest food web and potentially moving seeds.
species.pressures: Loss and fragmentation of wooded habitat, road traffic and disturbance can reduce safe movement and feeding areas.
species.watch: Observe quietly from a trail. Do not bait it with food or chase it into cover for a photograph.
species.fact: The pale stripe near its shoulder is a useful clue that it is not a squirrel.

funFacts.text: Treeshrews form their own mammal order, Scandentia.

species.name: False killer whale
species.habitat: Deep offshore seas and oceanic waters
species.rarity: Exceptional local record; the listing is not evidence of a resident population
species.summary: A large, dark oceanic dolphin whose name reflects a superficial resemblance to the killer whale. It is a member of the dolphin family.
species.identification: A long, dark grey to black body, rounded forehead, no distinct beak and narrow flippers with a characteristic forward bend. The dorsal fin is tall and curved.
species.diet: Large fish and cephalopods; some populations also take other marine mammals.
species.activity: An active offshore swimmer that must surface to breathe; Singapore-specific activity data are not established.
species.behaviour: Highly social and often travels in groups. Individuals may share prey, but behaviour varies among populations and encounters.
species.reproduction: Females bear a single calf after a long pregnancy and provide extended care. No Singapore breeding season is inferred from general species accounts.
species.singapore: NParks includes the false killer whale in the native marine-mammal list but records no Singapore RDB3 category for it. Rare occurrence should not be read as a population estimate.
species.ecologicalRole: A high-level predator in offshore marine food webs.
species.pressures: Fishing-gear interactions, prey depletion, contaminants, noise and mass-stranding events can affect the species.
species.watch: Never approach or attempt to refloat a stranded cetacean without trained responders. At sea, keep a steady course and give animals space.
species.fact: Despite its name, it is one of the larger members of the dolphin family.

funFacts.title: Built for open water

species.name: Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphin
species.habitat: Shallow tropical coasts, bays and estuaries
species.rarity: Rarely recorded locally; sightings do not establish abundance
species.sourceName: Animal Diversity Web · University of Michigan
species.summary: A coastal bottlenose dolphin of the Indo-Pacific. It resembles the better-known common bottlenose dolphin, so reliable identification needs more than a quick glimpse.
species.identification: A robust grey body, curved dorsal fin and a distinct medium-length beak. Adults may develop dark spotting on the underside; colour and spotting vary.
species.diet: A range of coastal fish, squid and other cephalopods.
species.activity: Travels, socialises and forages around the clock, with patterns shaped by prey and habitat.
species.behaviour: Lives in flexible social groups whose membership can change. Individuals use whistles and echolocation while navigating and finding prey.
species.reproduction: Usually one calf is born and remains dependent on its mother for an extended period. General timing must not be treated as a Singapore breeding forecast.
species.singapore: NParks lists this dolphin as native and Critically Endangered nationally. Singapore waters are part of a busy coastal system, and records do not guarantee a sighting at any named shore.
species.ecologicalRole: A mobile predator connecting fish communities across bays, estuaries and coastal waters.
species.pressures: Vessel strikes, entanglement, underwater noise, pollution, prey change and coastal development can affect bottlenose dolphins.
species.watch: Use binoculars from shore. On a vessel, do not cut across a group, follow closely, feed animals or separate a calf from adults.
species.fact: Adults can develop dark spots on the paler underside.

funFacts.title: Spots with age
funFacts.text: Some adults develop dark spotting on the underside as they mature.

funFacts.title: A sound-built map
funFacts.text: Bottlenose dolphins use echolocation clicks to investigate their surroundings and prey.

species.summary: A small coastal cetacean with a smooth back instead of a dorsal fin. It favours shallow waters that are also heavily used by people.

species.diet: Fish, shrimp, squid and other small aquatic prey.
species.activity: Makes short, often inconspicuous surfacings to breathe and may be active by day or night.

species.summary: A round-headed coastal dolphin recorded in Singapore waters. Despite its common name, it also uses marine and estuarine habitats rather than living only in rivers.
species.identification: A blunt, rounded forehead with no obvious beak, a small triangular dorsal fin and broad, rounded flippers. Colour is usually slate-grey, paler underneath.
species.diet: Fish, cephalopods and crustaceans captured in shallow water.
species.activity: Surfaces to breathe between dives; local daily activity patterns are not established in this guide.
species.behaviour: Usually seen in small groups. It is adapted to shallow, sometimes turbid water and may surface with a rolling movement that shows little of the body.
species.reproduction: Females give birth to a single calf and nurse it. Published species accounts describe slow reproduction; they do not establish a Singapore calving season.
species.singapore: NParks lists the Irrawaddy dolphin among Singapore's native marine mammals. A national listing confirms occurrence and risk category, not a predictable viewing site or resident population size.
species.ecologicalRole: A predator of fish and other aquatic prey in coastal and estuarine food webs.
species.pressures: Entanglement in fishing gear, vessel traffic, underwater noise, pollution and degradation of shallow-water habitat threaten populations across its range.
species.watch: Observe from shore where possible. Boats must not chase, encircle, feed or separate dolphins; report strandings to local wildlife authorities.
species.fact: Its rounded forehead meets the mouth without a long dolphin-like beak.

species.name: Large flying fox
species.habitat: Mangroves, coastal forest and tall communal roost trees
species.rarity: Rare and irregular in Singapore; roost locations are sensitive
species.sourceName: Animal Diversity Web · University of Michigan
species.summary: One of the world's largest bats, with a fox-like face and broad wings. It feeds on fruit and flowers and can move pollen and seeds over long distances.
species.identification: A very large dark-winged fruit bat with a long fox-like muzzle, large eyes and contrasting mantle around the shoulders. It has no tail.
species.activity: Nocturnal; leaves communal day roosts at dusk to forage across a wide area.
species.behaviour: Roosts in groups high in trees and can travel long distances between roosts and feeding sites. It relies strongly on sight and smell.
species.reproduction: Females generally bear one young and carry it when small. Life-history summaries do not establish local breeding dates or reveal roost sites.
species.singapore: NParks lists the large flying fox as native and Critically Endangered nationally. Records may involve mobile animals, and exact roost locations should not be publicised.
species.ecologicalRole: A long-distance pollinator and seed disperser that connects forest patches and coastal vegetation.
species.pressures: Roost loss and disturbance, hunting elsewhere in its range, loss of feeding trees and conflict around fruit crops threaten populations.
species.watch: Remain outside roost trees, keep noise and lights low and never fly drones near a colony. Do not handle grounded bats.
species.fact: Its broad wings carry pollen and seeds between places separated by many kilometres.

species.name: Lesser long-tongued nectar bat
species.habitat: Mangroves, coastal woodland, gardens and flowering vegetation
species.rarity: Uncommon and difficult to identify during brief night-time visits
species.sourceName: Animal Diversity Web · University of Michigan
species.summary: A small fruit bat with a long tongue adapted for sipping nectar. It uses coastal and wooded habitats where suitable flowers and roosts remain.
species.identification: A small brown fruit bat with a narrow elongated muzzle, large eyes, small ears and a very long brush-tipped tongue. Close identification should be left to specialists.
species.diet: Nectar and pollen, with soft fruit also taken.
species.activity: Nocturnal, visiting flowers after dusk and resting by day in foliage or sheltered vegetation.
species.behaviour: Often feeds alone at flowers and may hover briefly or cling while licking nectar. It carries pollen on its muzzle and fur.
species.reproduction: Females bear live young and nurse them. Published regional timing does not establish a Singapore season or roost location.
species.singapore: NParks lists the species as native and Vulnerable. Its use of mangroves and flowering vegetation makes coastal habitat quality important.
species.ecologicalRole: A nocturnal pollinator that links flowering plants across coastal and wooded habitats.
species.pressures: Mangrove loss, removal of night-flowering plants, roost disturbance and pesticide exposure can reduce food and shelter.
species.watch: Watch from a respectful distance without flash. Never disturb a day roost or pick up a bat with bare hands.
species.fact: A brush-tipped tongue helps collect nectar and pollen from flowers.

species.name: Sperm whale
species.habitat: Deep offshore seas and oceanic waters
species.rarity: Exceptional local record; not a predictable Singapore sighting
species.summary: The largest toothed whale, recognisable by its immense square head. A Singapore record documents occurrence, not a regular coastal population.
species.identification: A very large dark body, block-shaped head, low rounded dorsal hump and a blowhole offset to the left. The narrow lower jaw carries the visible functional teeth.
species.diet: Mainly squid, including deep-water species, as well as fish.
species.activity: Alternates long deep foraging dives with recovery periods at the surface.
species.behaviour: Females and young form social groups, while mature males may travel more widely. Echolocation clicks help whales navigate and hunt in darkness.
species.reproduction: A female gives birth to one calf after a long pregnancy and nurses it for years. No local breeding claim is made from a rare Singapore occurrence.
species.singapore: NParks includes the sperm whale on Singapore's native marine-mammal list without an assigned national risk category. An exceptional record must not be presented as a common resident.
species.ecologicalRole: A deep-diving predator that transfers energy through oceanic food webs and transports nutrients between depth and surface.
species.pressures: Entanglement, ship strikes, underwater noise, marine debris and contaminants can injure or displace sperm whales.
species.watch: Keep far away at sea and never approach a stranded whale. Contact local wildlife and maritime authorities and follow the cordon set by responders.
species.fact: It is the largest living toothed whale and specialises in deep dives.

after.name: Asian small-clawed otter
after.habitat: Mangroves, freshwater wetlands, streams and muddy banks
after.rarity: Rare in Singapore and much less often seen than the smooth-coated otter
after.sourceName: Animal Diversity Web · University of Michigan
after.summary: The world's smallest otter species, with dexterous front paws used to feel for small prey. It must not be confused with Singapore's larger, more familiar smooth-coated otter.
after.identification: A small dark-brown otter with a pale throat, short claws that do not extend beyond the fingertips and partly webbed paws. Size alone is not enough for a confident identification.
after.diet: Crabs, molluscs and other aquatic invertebrates, along with frogs and small fish.
after.activity: Can forage by day or night depending on disturbance, prey and local conditions.
after.behaviour: Social and vocal, often foraging with sensitive paws in mud and shallow water. Family groups use dens and scent-marked areas.
after.reproduction: A pair may raise a small litter with help from older group members. General species biology does not identify a Singapore den or breeding date.
after.singapore: NParks lists the native Asian small-clawed otter as Critically Endangered. Any suspected record should be documented from a distance and checked by specialists.
after.ecologicalRole: A predator of crabs, molluscs and other small wetland animals, linking shallow water and bank habitats.
after.pressures: Wetland loss, water pollution, road traffic, disturbance and illegal wildlife trade affect small-clawed otters across their range.

after.singapore: NParks lists the common treeshrew as native and Least Concern nationally. It depends on vegetated habitat even when a record comes from near a park edge.
after.ecologicalRole: An omnivore that eats small invertebrates and fruit, linking several parts of the forest food web and potentially moving seeds.
after.pressures: Loss and fragmentation of wooded habitat, road traffic and disturbance can reduce safe movement and feeding areas.
after.watch: Observe quietly from a trail. Do not bait it with food or chase it into cover for a photograph.
after.fact: The pale stripe near its shoulder is a useful clue that it is not a squirrel.

after.habitat: Shallow tropical coasts, bays and estuaries

after.summary: A coastal bottlenose dolphin of the Indo-Pacific. It resembles the better-known common bottlenose dolphin, so reliable identification needs more than a quick glimpse.
after.identification: A robust grey body, curved dorsal fin and a distinct medium-length beak. Adults may develop dark spotting on the underside; colour and spotting vary.
after.diet: A range of coastal fish, squid and other cephalopods.
after.activity: Travels, socialises and forages around the clock, with patterns shaped by prey and habitat.
after.behaviour: Lives in flexible social groups whose membership can change. Individuals use whistles and echolocation while navigating and finding prey.
after.reproduction: Usually one calf is born and remains dependent on its mother for an extended period. General timing must not be treated as a Singapore breeding forecast.
after.singapore: NParks lists this dolphin as native and Critically Endangered nationally. Singapore waters are part of a busy coastal system, and records do not guarantee a sighting at any named shore.
after.ecologicalRole: A mobile predator connecting fish communities across bays, estuaries and coastal waters.
after.pressures: Vessel strikes, entanglement, underwater noise, pollution, prey change and coastal development can affect bottlenose dolphins.
after.watch: Use binoculars from shore. On a vessel, do not cut across a group, follow closely, feed animals or separate a calf from adults.
after.fact: Adults can develop dark spots on the paler underside.

after.watch: Never chase or crowd a porpoise. Slow down in an encounter, keep a steady course, and contact trained authorities for any stranded animal.
after.fact: A low textured ridge replaces the dorsal fin found on most dolphins.

after.summary: The largest toothed whale, recognisable by its immense square head. A Singapore record documents occurrence, not a regular coastal population.

after.ecologicalRole: A deep-diving predator that transfers energy through oceanic food webs and transports nutrients between depth and surface.
after.pressures: Entanglement, ship strikes, underwater noise, marine debris and contaminants can injure or displace sperm whales.
after.watch: Keep far away at sea and never approach a stranded whale. Contact local wildlife and maritime authorities and follow the cordon set by responders.
after.fact: It is the largest living toothed whale and specialises in deep dives.
